::: {.callout-important}
## How to use this page

The TMUA gives you **no formula booklet and no calculator**, so everything here has to be *recalled*.

- **Part 1** is the reasoning core — sessions **S1–S7** compressed to what you must have automatic.
  There is **no symbol notation on the test**; it is all in English sentences. The arrows here are a
  thinking tool, not exam wording.
- **Parts 2 and 3** are the two **topics** that carry most of that reasoning: **divisors and primes**
  (fifteen-plus questions, 2016–2023) and **plane shapes asked as logical conditions** (every sitting).
- **Part 4** is the exam-day card.

Cards marked ★ appear on almost every paper. For the Paper 1 mathematics (MM1–MM8), use the
**[main formula sheet](../formula_sheet.qmd)**.
:::

---

# Part 1 · The reasoning core — S1 to S7

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Section 2 — Arg, Prf, Err</div>
<div class="fs-title">Logic and proof — the whole of it</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Seven cards. If you can reproduce these from memory you have the entire non-A-level content of Paper 2; everything else on the paper is Paper 1 mathematics wearing a logical wrapper.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### S1 · Statement forms ★

$$A\Rightarrow B\;=\;\text{“if }A\text{ then }B\text{”}\;=\;\text{“}A\text{ only if }B\text{”}\;=\;\text{“}B\text{ if }A\text{”}$$

**The bare "if" introduces the forcing statement.** So "$A$ **if** $B$" is $B\Rightarrow A$ — backwards from
the reading order.

"$A$ **if and only if** $B$" is both arrows: $A\Leftrightarrow B$.

**Reversed wording:** in "a condition **for** $Q$ is $P$", the target follows the word *for*. Find the
target first, then the condition.

[the trap: "only if" points forwards, "if" points backwards]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S2 · Converse and contrapositive ★

| | form | equivalent to the original? |
|---|---|---|
| statement | $A\Rightarrow B$ | — |
| **converse** | $B\Rightarrow A$ | **no** |
| inverse | $\lnot A\Rightarrow\lnot B$ | **no** |
| **contrapositive** | $\lnot B\Rightarrow\lnot A$ | **always yes** |

The inverse and the converse are contrapositives *of each other*, so they stand or fall together.

When a question asks **"which must be true"**, the answer is almost always the contrapositive and the
**converse is the trap option**.

[negate a compound with De Morgan — see S4]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S3 · Necessary and sufficient ★

$$\text{“}P\text{ sufficient for }Q\text{”}=P\Rightarrow Q\qquad
\text{“}P\text{ necessary for }Q\text{”}=Q\Rightarrow P$$

**Sufficient points forwards; necessary points backwards.**

**The routine that answers every one of these.** Write the *exact* set of cases making each statement
true, then compare by inclusion:

$$P\subset Q\Rightarrow\textbf{sufficient, not necessary}\qquad
Q\subset P\Rightarrow\textbf{necessary, not sufficient}$$
$$P=Q\Rightarrow\textbf{both}\qquad\text{overlapping}\Rightarrow\textbf{neither}$$

[25 % of recent papers — the largest single block of marks]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S4 · Quantifiers and negation ★

$$\lnot(\forall x,\;P)=\exists x,\;\lnot P\qquad\lnot(\exists x,\;P)=\forall x,\;\lnot P$$

The negation of "**all** X are Y" is "**some** X is **not** Y" — *not* "no X is Y".

**De Morgan.** $\lnot(P\text{ and }Q)=\lnot P\text{ or }\lnot Q$; $\lnot(P\text{ or }Q)=\lnot P\text{ and }\lnot Q$.

**Negating an implication.** $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P\text{ **and** }\lnot Q$ — never "if $P$ then not $Q$".

**Order matters.** $\forall x\,\exists y$ lets $y$ depend on $x$; $\exists y\,\forall x$ needs one $y$ for
all $x$ at once — far stronger.

[to negate a chain, flip every quantifier in order, then the inside]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S5 · Proof methods

- **Direct** — assume the hypothesis, deduce the conclusion. Represent generally ($2k$, $2k+1$).
- **By cases** — split by remainder; check every case.
- **By contradiction** — assume the negation, derive an absurdity.
- **By counterexample** — to disprove "for all", one case is enough.

**A counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis *and* fail the conclusion.** A case where the hypothesis
fails proves nothing.

**"Possible" is $\exists$** — produce one witness. **"Must" is $\forall$** — one counterexample destroys it.

[read which one you were given before starting]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S6 · Scrambled proofs

Anchor the ends, then follow the dependencies.

1. **First line** introduces notation or assumes the hypothesis ("Let…", "Suppose…").
2. **Last line** states the conclusion, or the contradiction.
3. A line can only come after every line it **uses**.
4. Connecting words carry the order: *therefore*, *hence*, *so*, *it follows*.

**Build the chain yourself before reading the options** — the distractors are a tidy but wrong parallel
chain, so comparing them directly is slower and riskier.

[rare: one TMUA question in eight years, 2016 P2 Q7]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### S7 · Spot the error ★

Read downwards; stop at the **first** line that fails.

1. **Small cases** — does it survive $n=1$, $x=0$, the empty case?
2. **Dividing** — could the divisor be $0$? $ab=ac\Rightarrow b=c$ needs $a\neq0$.
3. **Squaring** — invents roots; $\sqrt X<Y$ silently needs $Y>0$.
4. **Reversing** — did it use the **converse** of what was proved?
5. **For all vs there exists** — an example never proves a "for all".
6. **$\sin A=\sin B\Rightarrow A=B$** is invalid.
7. **Log with base $<1$ reverses the inequality.**

*Sometimes the honest answer is "no error".*

[exactly 1–3 per paper, every year since 2016]{.eg}
:::

# Part 2 · T1 — Divisors and primes

*Fifteen-plus Paper 2 questions across 2016–2023, and **not one of them a calculation**. The mathematics is
tiny and repeats; learn it cold. Full page: **[T1](t01_divisors_primes.qmd)**.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Topic T1</div>
<div class="fs-title">Divisors &amp; primes — the memorisable core</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Every card has a standard counterexample attached. Learn the counterexample with the fact — that is what the questions actually test.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Primes and the $6n\pm1$ form ★

Every prime $>3$ is of the form $6n\pm1$, because $6n$, $6n\pm2$ and $6n+3$ all carry a factor of $2$ or $3$.

**The converse is false:** $25$, $35$, $49$, $55$ are all $6n\pm1$ and none is prime.

**Edge cases that break proofs:** $1$ is **not** prime; $2$ is the **only** even prime; $3k$ is composite
**only when $k>1$**, since $3\times1=3$ is prime.

[$n^{2}+2$ is prime at $n=1$ — that single case kills several textbook "proofs"]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Euclid's lemma — the missing word ★

$$p\mid ab\;\Longrightarrow\;p\mid a\ \text{ or }\ p\mid b\qquad\textbf{only if }p\textbf{ is prime}$$

**Drop "prime" and it collapses:** $4\mid2\times2$ but $4\nmid2$. Smallest counterexample $a=4,\ b=c=2$.

[2016 P2 Q13 and 2021 P2 Q4 are the *same* false statement — this is the word they removed]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Squaring doubles every exponent ★

$n=p_1^{e_1}p_2^{e_2}\cdots\Rightarrow n^{2}=p_1^{2e_1}p_2^{2e_2}\cdots$, so $n^{2}$ carries only **even**
powers.

For a **prime** $p$: $p\mid n^{2}\Rightarrow p\mid n$. For a composite divisor you only recover its square
root:
$$12\mid n^{2}\iff 6\mid n\qquad(\textbf{not }12\mid n) .$$

**Counterexample:** $n=6$ gives $n^{2}=36=12\times3$, yet $12\nmid6$.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Remainders, and what squares leave

"$b$ leaves remainder $r$ on division by $a$" means $b=aq+r$ **with $0\le r<a$** — the size condition is
half the definition.

**Trap:** if $r,s<a$ the product $rs$ need **not** be $<a$, so $rs$ is not the remainder of $bc$. Take
$a=4$, $r=s=2$: $rs=4$, true remainder $0$.

$$n^{2}\equiv0,1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 3)\qquad n^{2}\equiv0,1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 4)\qquad n^{2}\equiv0,1,4\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 8)$$

A square is **never** $2\bmod3$ and **never** $3\bmod4$.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The gcd toolkit

$$\gcd(a,b)\mid a\pm b\qquad \gcd(a,\,b+ka)=\gcd(a,b)\qquad \gcd(n,\,n+1)=1$$

If $\gcd(a,b)=d$ then $d$ divides **every** combination $xa+yb$ — which is why a common factor survives all
the way down a recurrence.

[$\gcd(a,b)=7$ with $u_{n+2}=u_n+u_{n+1}$ forces $7\mid u_n$ for every $n$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Irreducible $\neq$ prime-valued ★

A polynomial that does not factorise over the integers still takes **composite values**.

$3x^{2}+3x+1$ is irreducible ($D=9-12=-3<0$), yet $x=5$ gives $91=7\times13$ — which is exactly
$6^{3}-5^{3}$.

**No non-constant polynomial takes only prime values**, so any claim of that shape is false before you read
its proof.

**Two meanings of "factor":** a divisor of an **integer**, and a factor of a **polynomial**. The examiners
slide between them deliberately.
:::

::::

:::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The two reflexes for this topic

1. **Test $n=1,2,3,4$ before reasoning.** For $n^{3}+5n$ that gives $6,18,42,84$ — one line of arithmetic
   that eliminates five of seven options.
2. **Check the smallest allowed case of every "therefore it is composite" step.** Almost every flawed proof
   in this topic is correct for large $n$ and dies at the boundary.
:::

# Part 3 · T2 — Shapes as logical conditions

*Eight sittings, eight appearances. The geometry never goes beyond GCSE; what is tested is which property
forces which, and whether you can produce the standard counterexample on demand. Full page:
**[T2](t02_shapes_as_logic.qmd)**.*

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Topic T2</div>
<div class="fs-title">Shapes as logical conditions</div>
<div class="fs-sub">The lattice, the diagonal table, the congruence criteria and the three counterexamples. Learn the <strong>arrows</strong>: every question here is asking you to read one off, usually backwards.</div>
::::

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### The quadrilateral lattice ★

$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rhombus}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}\Rightarrow\text{trapezium}$$
$$\text{square}\Rightarrow\text{rectangle}\Rightarrow\text{parallelogram}$$

A square is **both** a rhombus and a rectangle; nothing else is. A **kite** sits outside the chain unless it
is a rhombus.

*Arrows run one way only* — reading one backwards is what every wrong option in this topic does.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The three counterexamples ★

- **rhombus** — equal sides, perpendicular diagonals, **not a square**
- **rectangle** — equal diagonals, right angles, **not a square**
- **isosceles trapezium** — one pair parallel, other pair equal, **not a parallelogram**

Almost every "is this sufficient?" question is killed by one of these three. *Reach for a named shape
before you try to prove anything.*
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The diagonal table — these are the *iff*s ★

| diagonals | shape guaranteed |
|---|---|
| bisect each other | parallelogram |
| bisect **and equal** | rectangle |
| bisect **and perpendicular** | rhombus |
| bisect, equal **and** perpendicular | square |
| one perpendicularly bisects the other | kite |

Read each as **at least** that shape — a square satisfies every row. Most nec/suff options on the paper are
one of these rows, altered.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Forcing a parallelogram

**Sufficient, each alone:** both pairs of sides parallel · both pairs equal · the **same one pair** both
equal **and** parallel · diagonals bisect each other.

**Not sufficient — the exam's favourite:** one pair *equal* and a **different** pair *parallel*
($AB=CD$ but $AD\parallel BC$). That describes an **isosceles trapezium**.

*Splitting "equal" and "parallel" across different pairs is the whole trap.*
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Congruence, and the one that is not ★

**Criteria:** SSS · SAS · ASA · AAS · RHS.

**SSA is not a criterion** — two sides and a *non-included* angle give the ambiguous case, two triangles.

**Equal area is not a criterion either:** $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ equal gives only $\sin C_1=\sin C_2$, and

$$\sin A=\sin B\iff B=A\ \text{ or }\ B=180^\circ-A .$$

*Whenever an angle is recovered from a sine, stop — there are two possibilities.*
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Polygons and circles

$$\text{interior sum}=(n-2)\times180^\circ\qquad\text{regular interior}=180^\circ-\frac{360^\circ}{n}$$

$n=3,4,5,6,8,12\Rightarrow60^\circ,90^\circ,108^\circ,120^\circ,135^\circ,150^\circ$.

**Pentagon consequence:** five angles in arithmetic progression sum to $5a=540^\circ$, so the **middle one
is forced to be $108^\circ$**, whatever the common difference.

**Equal areas from the centre $\neq$ regular:** each central angle is $\alpha$ or $180^\circ-\alpha$, so
only $n=3$ forces regularity. For $n=4$, angles $60,120,60,120$ work.

**Cyclic quadrilateral:** opposite angles sum to $180^\circ$ — a genuine *iff*.
:::

::::

# Part 4 · The exam-day card

::: {.callout-important}
## Before you read a single question

Write these at the top of your rough paper:

1. $\;$ **sufficient $\to$ forwards, necessary $\to$ backwards**
2. $\;$ **contrapositive = equivalent; converse = trap**
3. $\;$ $\lnot(P\Rightarrow Q)=P$ **and** $\lnot Q$
4. $\;$ **rhombus · rectangle · isosceles trapezium** — the three counterexamples
5. $\;$ $p\mid ab\Rightarrow p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$ — **only for prime $p$**
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The thirty-second routine for any Paper 2 question

**Name the reasoning type first, then do the mathematics.** Almost every lost mark comes from competent
mathematics done on the wrong question.

| The question says… | It is asking for… | So you… |
|---|---|---|
| "necessary", "sufficient" | set inclusion | find the **exact** set, then compare |
| "must be true" | $\forall$ | find a counterexample, or prove it |
| "possible", "can" | $\exists$ | **produce one witness** |
| "which is equivalent" | contrapositive | negate both halves and reverse |
| "first error", "best describes" | Err1/Err2 | read down, stop at the first failure |
| no logical wording at all | Paper 1 technique | just calculate — about a quarter of the paper |
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Where the marks are, from eight years of papers.** Necessary/sufficient **25 %** · straight calculation
**28 %** · quantifiers **15 %** · spot the error **10 %** · converse/contrapositive **8 %** ·
counterexample **7 %**. Divisors and primes carry about **13 %** of the questions, and a plane shape asked
as a logical condition appears in **every** sitting.
:::
